title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
Linear algebra appears whenever constraints are linear, path choices form an XOR space, spanning trees must be counted, or a long recurrence must be compressed. Always identify the scalar domain first: real numbers, \(\mathbb F_p\), and \(\mathbb F_2\) have different numerical and structural hazards.


Over a field, row operations preserve the solution set. Maintain a pivot row \(r\); for each column choose a nonzero entry, swap it to \(r\), normalize, and eliminate. Rank is the number of pivots. A zero row with a nonzero augmented entry means inconsistency; otherwise there are \(m-\operatorname{rank}\) free variables.
This is \(O(nm\min(n,m))\). For determinant, do not normalize: each row swap negates the answer, multiply by the pivot, then eliminate below using a[i][c]/pivot. Composite moduli are not fields: a nonzero pivot may be noninvertible. Use prime-factor methods, fraction-free elimination, or exact integer algorithms instead.
Worked example. Over \(\mathbb F_5\), \(x+y=1\), \(2x+3y=0\). Subtract twice the first row from the second: \(y=3\); hence \(x=3\). The integer solution is irrelevant—the field is part of the problem.



A set of machine words is a vector set whose coordinates are bits. Keep at most one pivot per highest bit.
Insertion costs \(O(B)\). If rank is \(r\), the span has \(2^{r}\) distinct values. For representation counts from \(n\) input vectors, every reachable value has \(2^{n-r}\) representations. To obtain the k-th smallest XOR, first reduce to a canonical basis (eliminate pivot bits in both directions); a merely triangular basis is insufficient.
Graph recognition: assign each vertex an XOR distance from a DFS root. Every non-tree edge yields a cycle XOR dist[u] ^ w ^ dist[v]. If \(s,t\) lie in the same undirected connected component, all XORs of walks from \(s\) to \(t\) are dist[s]^dist[t] plus the span of that component’s cycle XORs.



For a weighted undirected graph, form the Laplacian
\[L_{ii}=\sum_{j\ne i}w_{ij},\qquad L_{ij}=-w_{ij}\quad(i\ne j).\]
Delete any one row and the corresponding column. The determinant of the resulting \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) cofactor equals the total weight of spanning trees, where a tree’s weight is the product of its edge weights.
Why it works: orient edges arbitrarily and let \(B\) be the incidence matrix. Then \(L=BWB^{T}\). Cauchy–Binet expands a cofactor determinant over edge subsets; exactly the spanning trees have determinant squared equal to one. Directed arborescences use an in- or out-Laplacian—choose the convention from the desired root orientation and test it on two vertices.
Complexity is \(O(n^{3})\) with dense elimination. Parallel edge weights add. Self-loops do not contribute. Under a modulus, the determinant counts modulo that modulus.



If \(s_n=c_1s_{n-1}+\cdots+c_ks_{n-k}\), then \(x^{k}-c_1x^{k-1}-\cdots-c_k\) annihilates the sequence. To find \(s_N\), reduce \(x^{N}\) modulo this polynomial, then combine the first \(k\) terms. Binary exponentiation with polynomial reduction costs \(O(k^{2}\log N)\) (Kitamasa); NTT-based methods or Bostan–Mori improve large \(k\).
Berlekamp–Massey recovers the shortest recurrence from about twice as many terms over a field. Preconditions: exact field arithmetic and enough terms; a short prefix can admit a spurious recurrence.
Cayley–Hamilton says a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial. Thus every scalar sequence \(u^T A^n v\) has order at most the matrix dimension. This bridges matrix exponentiation, recurrences, and generating functions.



For dense matrices, Hessenberg reduction followed by the determinant recurrence computes the characteristic polynomial in \(O(n^{3})\). Determinant interpolation at \(n+1\) points is simpler but \(O(n^{4})\) with naive determinants.
For a huge sparse matrix, Wiedemann chooses random vectors \(u,v\), generates \(a_i=u^T A^i v\), and applies Berlekamp–Massey. With enough terms, this recovers the scalar sequence’s minimal polynomial exactly; random projection makes it equal to the matrix’s minimal polynomial with high probability, with a bound that depends on the field and invariant factors. Applications include sparse linear systems and determinants after random diagonal preconditioning.
Assumptions and failure modes:

It is randomized; a projection can miss invariant factors. Repeat independently.
Field size should be comfortably large. Extension fields or several primes reduce failure probability.
One sparse matrix-vector multiply must be fast; otherwise dense elimination is safer.
Recovering a determinant requires more than the scalar recurrence: use a proven preconditioning recipe and account for the preconditioner’s determinant.





Division modulo a composite number silently invalidates Gaussian elimination.
Partial pivoting is essential over floating point, but “largest pivot” has no meaning in a finite field.
A determinant changes sign on every row swap.
A graph XOR basis uses cycle values, not raw edge weights.
Kirchhoff counts multigraph edges separately; collapsing them without adding weights changes the answer.
Berlekamp–Massey coefficient sign conventions differ among templates. Verify on Fibonacci before a contest.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
This chapter is the bridge from “know the formula” to derive the formula under contest pressure. It assumes factorials, binomial coefficients and elementary inclusion–exclusion (IE). Read it before group actions and generating functions.









Wording in a statement
First model to try




every required property is present
IE over missing properties


exactly/at least \(k\) properties
binomial inversion or weighted IE


partition labelled objects into unlabeled nonempty groups
Stirling numbers of the second kind


cycles of a permutation
unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind


recursively nested / balanced / plane tree
Catalan family

binomial transform


constraints are local but labels are global
combinatorial class + EGF



Always write what one object is, what is labelled, and whether order matters. Most wrong generating functions arise before any algebra is performed.



For bad events \(E_1,\ldots,E_m\), attach a set \(B(x)\subseteq[m]\) of bad properties to each object. Then
\[
  \mathbf 1[B(x)=\varnothing]=\sum_{S\subseteq B(x)}(-1)^{|S|}.
\]
Summing this identity over objects proves IE and is more robust than memorising signs. If \(f(S)\) counts objects having every bad property in \(S\), the answer is \(\sum_S(-1)^{|S|}f(S)\). Symmetry often collapses \(2^{m}\) terms into \(m+1\): if \(f(S)=g(|S|)\), use \(\sum_k(-1)^{k}{m\choose k}g(k)\).


Let \(a_j\) count objects satisfying exactly \(j\) conditions and let \(b_k=\sum_{|S|=k}f(S)\). Double counting pairs (object, chosen k true conditions) gives
\[
b_k=\sum_{j\ge k}{j\choose k}a_j,
\qquad
a_r=\sum_{k\ge r}(-1)^{k-r}{k\choose r}b_k.
\]
This is binomial inversion. The common transforms \(b_n=\sum_{k\le n}{n\choose k}a_k\) and \(a_n=\sum_{k\le n}(-1)^{n-k}{n\choose k}b_k\) follow similarly.






\[
{n\brace k}=k{n-1\brace k}+{n-1\brace k-1},\qquad
{n\brack k}=(n-1){n-1\brack k}+{n-1\brack k-1}.
\]
The first recurrence puts label \(n\) into one of \(k\) blocks or makes a new block. The second inserts it after one of \(n-1\) existing permutation elements, or creates a new cycle. Useful closed transforms are
\[
{n\brace k}=\frac1{k!}\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^{k-i}{k\choose i}i^n,
\quad x^{\overline n}=\sum_k {n\brack k}x^k.
\]
Bell numbers satisfy \(B_n=\sum_k{n\brace k}\). Their EGF is \(\exp(e^{x}-1)\): a partition is a labelled set of nonempty labelled sets.



A plane rooted binary object is empty or a root with an ordered pair of such objects, so \(C(x)=1+xC(x)^{2}\). Hence
\[
C_n=\frac1{n+1}{2n\choose n},\qquad
C_{n+1}=\sum_{i=0}^n C_iC_{n-i}.
\]
Equivalent objects include Dyck paths, balanced parentheses, triangulations, and binary-search-tree shapes. Do not apply Catalan merely because parentheses appear: check that the first-return decomposition is independent.



For unlimited parts, mark total size:
\[
P(x)=\prod_{j\ge1}(1-x^j)^{-1}.
\]
Restricting parts to a set deletes factors; allowing each at most once changes the factor to \(1+x^{j}\). Euler’s pentagonal recurrence computes all \(p(n)\) in \(O(N\sqrt N)\):
\[
p(n)=\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^{k-1}
\left(p(n-k(3k-1)/2)+p(n-k(3k+1)/2)\right).
\]




Many triangular sums become one convolution. For example,
\[
b_n=\sum_{k=0}^n {n\choose k}a_k
=n!\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{a_k}{k!}\frac1{(n-k)!}.
\]
Convolve \(A_k=a_k/k!\) and \(F_k=1/k!\), then multiply coefficient \(n\) by \(n!\). This is \(O(N\log N)\) with NTT. The formula requires all required factorials to be invertible; normally use a prime modulus with \(N<p\).
Stirling columns can also be obtained by convolution from the explicit formula. For all \({n\brace k}\) at one fixed \(n\), convolve \(A_i=(-1)^{i}/i!\) and \(B_i=i^{n}/i!\); the coefficient at \(k\) is \({n\brace k}\).



For permutations avoiding forbidden cells, place nonattacking rooks in the forbidden board. If \(r_k\) is the number of ways to choose \(k\) mutually compatible forbidden assignments, IE yields
\[
  \sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k r_k(n-k)!.
\]
Disconnected boards multiply rook polynomials. This turns some intimidating IE into polynomial products over small components.



Example: surjections. Count functions \([n] \to  [k]\) using every target. Choose \(i\) omitted targets and apply IE: \(\sum_i(-1)^{i}{k\choose i}(k-i)^{n}=k!{n\brace k}\). This simultaneously explains the Stirling explicit formula: a partition into \(k\) nonempty fibers, then an ordering of the fibers.
Frequent bugs:

confusing labelled blocks (\(k! {n\brace k}\)) with unlabeled blocks;
dividing by \(k!\) when the modulus does not permit it;
using a closed form whose range crosses the characteristic;
performing IE over constraints although intersections are not easier;
silently counting rotations/reflections as distinct (see chapter 05).

title: 13 — Mixed Mathematics Capstones
text:
These problems come last because the main difficulty is classification. Nothing in a World Finals statement announces “use a formal logarithm” or “perform Möbius inversion on this poset.” A capstone attempt should therefore begin without opening the topic tags in this repository.


Before coding, write answers to these questions:

What is the mathematical object: residue class, multiplicative function, polynomial/FPS, labelled class, group action, linear operator, random variable, or lattice sum?
Which operation is expensive: pairwise product, convolution, coefficient extraction, repeated transition, divisor sum, or enumeration of symmetric copies?
Which change of basis makes that operation pointwise or triangular?
What is the coefficient ring, and which divisions/roots actually exist?
What brute-force oracle can test the first 20–100 cases?

The ordered set below revisits a few chapter problems in a deliberately tag-free setting and adds one synthesis problem. Treat each as a 3–5 hour team session, not a normal single-person rating drill.




Do not inspect tags, hints, or editorials for the first 90 minutes.
At 90 minutes, compare the three best models you considered. Open only Hint 1 if none gives the target complexity.
At 150 minutes, open Hint 2 and require a written derivation before coding.
At 210 minutes, open Hint 3. Stop after five hours and study the official analysis; continuing an unproductive implementation is not endurance training.
Re-solve from a blank file six weeks later. A remembered code template does not count unless you can re-derive its contract.

Statement · official editorial · English/Japanese
Prerequisites: cyclic multiplicative groups, primitive roots, convolution.
Why here: the hard step is recognizing that a group isomorphism turns a distribution of products into additive convolution.



Hint 1 — recognition

Nonzero residues modulo the fixed prime form a cyclic group.



Hint 2 — reduction

Map each value to its discrete-log index under a primitive root; multiplication becomes cyclic addition of indices.



Hint 3 — algorithm

Convolve the frequency array, fold indices modulo (p-1), then remove diagonal and ordering contributions carefully.





Statement · official analysis · English/Russian
Prerequisites: LCM bounds, linear congruences, generalized CRT.
Why here: a local gcd pattern must first be converted into compatible global row/column congruences, then checked against construction bounds.



Hint 1

Choose a row divisible by every requested entry.



Hint 2

Each desired gcd imposes a congruence on the starting column modulo that entry.



Hint 3

Merge non-coprime congruences, then verify every gcd explicitly; CRT consistency alone is not the full proof.





Statement · official Hello 2019 editorial · English/Russian
Prerequisites: divisor zeta/Möbius transforms and arithmetic over \(\mathbb F_2\).
Why here: it combines a non-obvious coordinate system with a representation chosen specifically for a million online operations.



Hint 1

Query parity suggests storing every multiset in a vector space over \(\mathbb F_2\).



Hint 2

Find a transform in which multiset union is addition and the pairwise-GCD product is pointwise multiplication.



Hint 3

Use divisor-incidence vectors packed into bitsets; derive the inverse coefficient needed to recover one exact value.





Statement · GF/FPS derivation · English
Prerequisites: combinatorial decomposition, NTT, FPS inverse and square root.
Why here: the combinatorial equation is short; recognizing and safely computing its algebraic solution is the real test.



Hint 1

Write a generating function for the allowed root weights and decompose a tree at its root.



Hint 2

The two ordered child slots produce a quadratic functional equation.



Hint 3

Select the formal root with the correct constant term and evaluate it using FPS square root and inverse, truncated after every operation.





Statement · official tutorial · English/Russian
Prerequisites: tree counting, polynomial-valued DP, finite differences or interpolation.
Why here: it requires proving that a huge-domain answer is a low-degree polynomial before any fast evaluation is possible.



Hint 1

Parameterize a subtree by the largest label it may use.



Hint 2

Children multiply; adding the parent takes a prefix sum, so track how the polynomial degree changes.



Hint 3

Compute enough consecutive values and evaluate the resulting bounded-degree polynomial at the large argument.





Statement · official editorial, JA
Prerequisites: Burnside, conjugacy classes of \(S_n\), integer partitions, induced permutation actions.
Why here: applying Burnside is easy; compressing \(n!\) group elements and counting edge orbits is the mastery step.



Hint 1

Graphs are subsets of unordered vertex pairs, acted on by relabeling vertices.



Hint 2

Group vertex permutations by cycle type rather than enumerating them.



Hint 3

For each vertex cycle type, count cycles in the induced action on unordered pairs; an invariant edge set is constant on each induced cycle.





Statement · official tutorial · English/Russian
Prerequisites: ranked subset convolution and AND/OR/XOR transforms.
Why here: the expression must be separated into several distributions, each diagonalized by a different transform, then recombined without losing ordered multiplicities.



Hint 1

Replace indices by a frequency distribution over their bitmask values.



Hint 2

Construct the OR-with-disjointness, singleton, and XOR distributions separately.



Hint 3

Apply the appropriate transform to each stage, include the Fibonacci weights at the right time, and audit whether tuples are ordered.





Statement, ZH · solution index, ZH
Prerequisites: gcd extraction, totient identities, weighted summatory functions, Du Jiao recursion, quotient blocks.
Why here: several familiar identities must be composed before the desired summatory function even becomes visible.



Hint 1

Extract the gcd in the double sum and rewrite the coprime part with a totient identity.



Hint 2

Identify the weighted totient prefix that the quotient blocks require.



Hint 3

Derive a convolution recurrence for that prefix, evaluate polynomial block sums exactly, and remember that the modulus need not justify division.





Finish at least six of the eight, including one of Problems 6–8, under the timed rules. For the remaining problems, a complete postmortem after studying the editorial is preferable to copying an implementation. Then run one five-hour virtual ICPC or Universal Cup contest and classify every unsolved mathematics problem against the dependency map in the root README.

title: 17 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization
text:
Determinants encode signed cycle covers. Choosing the matrix entries carefully makes unwanted covers cancel, leaving spanning trees, matchings, or parity structures. Random evaluation then turns a symbolic nonzeroness question into finite-field linear algebra.


For an even-dimensional skew-symmetric matrix \(A\), the Pfaffian sums signed products over perfect pairings and satisfies
\[\operatorname{Pf}(A)^{2}=\det A.\]
Eliminate pairs of rows/columns together. If pivot A[i][j] is used, swap indices into the active pair, account for the Pfaffian sign, multiply the pivot, and apply the skew-symmetric Schur-complement update. This is \(O(n^{3})\) over a field of characteristic not two. The hafnian removes signs and directly counts weighted perfect pairings, but its general algorithms are exponential.



For an undirected graph, put an indeterminate \(x_{ij}\) above the diagonal, \(-x_{ij}\) below it, and zero on nonedges. Its determinant is a nonzero polynomial iff the graph has a perfect matching. Substituting independent uniform field values from a set \(S\) gives a one-sided-error \(O(n^{3})\) test: for an \(n\)-vertex graph, a false negative has probability at most \(n/|S|\) per trial. Likewise, the evaluated matrix rank is twice the maximum matching size with high probability. The symbolic theorem is valid in characteristic two as well, but sampling only from \(\mathbb F_2\) gives a useless error bound; use a sufficiently large field or extension field.



A nonzero polynomial of total degree \(d\) evaluated uniformly over a finite set \(S\) vanishes with probability at most \(d/|S|\). Record all three quantities: degree, field size, and number of trials. Random evaluation can produce a false zero but never a false symbolic witness. Use fresh randomness, avoid tiny fields, and repeat when the error budget is not negligible.



\(det(A+xB)\) packages a family of rank/determinant questions into one polynomial; evaluate at enough field points and interpolate. The matrix determinant lemma and Sherman–Morrison give rank-one updates when the required inverse exists. The adjugate identity
\[A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)I\]
remains meaningful when \(A\) is singular and is often the safer symbolic object.




Capstone — Degree Harmony, ABC412 G. Weighted matching through determinant polynomials.


Hints

Reduce the degree constraints to a minimum-weight perfect matching; encode weights as powers of a new variable and recover the lowest nonzero degree.

Alternate-method lab — No Need, ABC056 D. Polynomial fingerprints.


Hints

Card \(i\) is necessary exactly when a subset of the other cards has sum in \([K-a_i,K)\). Replace each factor by \(1+r_jx^{a_j}\), multiply modulo \(x^K\), and divide by \(1+r_ix^{a_i}\) to exclude card \(i\). Distinct subsets give distinct square-free monomials in the formal variables \(r_j\), so the relevant coefficient polynomial cannot cancel identically. Independent uniform substitutions in \(\mathbb F_P\) turn this into a Monte Carlo test; bound the error over all tested coefficients with Schwartz–Zippel and a union bound (the official analysis obtains \(O(N^2/P)\)).

title: Advanced Mathematics for ICPC
text:
Build the recognition, derivation, and modelling skills behind hard competitive-programming mathematics. The course assumes you already have a tested implementation library and focuses on deciding what to apply and why it works.
Start with the prerequisite audit or open the study plan.
This is a dependency-guided course for an experienced competitive programmer who already solves around Codeforces 2200 level. It is deliberately biased toward techniques that turn a difficult mathematical observation into an implementable algorithm. Geometry is out of scope.
The notes assume that the reader already has a comprehensive, tested algorithm library. They focus on contracts, derivations, recognition clues, and failure modes rather than reproducing standard implementations. Code appears only when a non-standard snippet materially clarifies an idea. Shared symbols and preconditions are collected in notation reference.

title: Advanced Mathematics for ICPC
text:
How to use the course

Take the prerequisite audit. Patch only the gaps it exposes.
Read a chapter’s theory before opening its problem hints.
Attempt each problem for 60–120 minutes. Open Hint 1 only when you cannot name the relevant mathematical object; open Hint 2 only when the reduction remains unclear; use Hint 3 when you know the mathematics but cannot obtain the target complexity.
After solving, write a three-line postmortem: recognition clue, decisive identity, and the implementation hazard you would miss next time.
Re-solve Mastery and Capstone problems after two and six weeks.

For a concrete multi-month cadence, use the optional 24-week study plan.
Problem levels used throughout the repository are local to this course:

Foundation isolates one prerequisite or modelling step.
Advanced combines a central theorem with a standard algorithm.
Mastery hides the model or requires a non-obvious transformation.
Capstone combines several chapters or is appropriate team-contest work.

text:
Source and spoiler policy
Statements are linked, not copied. The notes paraphrase the mathematical idea and give layered hints rather than complete solutions to listed exercises. Official statements and editorials are preferred; high-quality community tutorials are used where they explain a theorem better. A language label is shown when a useful source is not English. See the sources page for the source hierarchy and durable reference material.
No collection can guarantee that a future ICPC problem will not introduce new mathematics. The goal here is stronger and more realistic: build the common toolkit, the habit of deriving missing variants, and enough hard practice that a new statement can be reduced to familiar algebra under contest pressure.

title: 09 — Transforms on Subsets and Divisors
text:
This chapter is about changing coordinates. A convolution that appears quadratic often becomes pointwise multiplication after the correct transform. The central habit is to identify the underlying partially ordered set (poset): subset inclusion, divisibility, or the Boolean group under XOR.


For a function \(f[S]\) on subsets of an \(n\)-element universe, the subset zeta transform is
\[F[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f[T].\]
Process one bit at a time, adding the state without the current bit into the state with it; invert by subtracting in the same schedule. After processing bits \(0,\ldots,i\), the current value has summed over all ways of deleting those bits. This induction invariant explains the transform—not merely its loop pattern.
Both take \(O(n2^{n})\) time and \(O(1)\) extra memory. The inverse works because the Möbius function of the Boolean lattice is \(\mu(T,S)=(-1)^{|S\setminus T|}\). The bits may be processed in any order because their stages commute. Keep one bit as the outer stage, however, and invert each butterfly \((a,b)\mapsto(a,a+b)\) with \((a,b)\mapsto(a,b-a)\); changing which member of the pair receives the update changes the transform.
The superset variants switch the condition and update f[s] += f[s | 1<<b]. Recognition signals include “sum over all submasks/supermasks”, compatibility masks, and inclusion–exclusion over missing features.


For \(h[S]=\sum_{A\cup B=S}f[A]g[B]\), subset-zeta both arrays, multiply pointwise, then subset-Möbius. For \(A\cap B=S\), use superset-zeta instead. Complexity is \(O(n2^{n})\).




XOR masks form the group \((\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^{n}\). Its characters are \(\chi_k(x)=(-1)^{\langle k,x\rangle}\). Therefore
\[\widehat f[k]=\sum_x f[x]\chi_k(x),\qquad
\widehat{f *_\oplus g}[k]=\widehat f[k]\widehat g[k].\]
The Walsh–Hadamard butterfly evaluates these characters recursively.
For an array of length \(N=2^n\), XOR inversion divides by \(N\). Thus the coefficient ring must make \(N\) invertible; over a field this is equivalent to characteristic not two. Under an odd prime modulus multiply by \(N^{-1}\). With integers, transform, multiply using a wide type, then divide exactly on inversion. OR/AND FWT uses triangular butterflies and has no normalization.
Worked example. With \(f[0]=1,f[1]=2\) and \(g[0]=3,g[1]=4\), the XOR convolution is \([1·3+2·4, 1·4+2·3]=[11,10]\). Their transforms are \([3,-1]\) and \([7,-1]\); pointwise product \([21,1]\), inverse butterfly gives \([11,10]\).



The disjoint-union convolution is
\[h[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f[T]g[S\setminus T].\]
Plain enumeration costs \(O(3^{n})\). Split each array by rank: \(f_k[S]=f[S]\) if \(|S|=k\), else zero. Zeta-transform every rank, form
\[H_k[S]=\sum_{i=0}^{k} F_i[S]G_{k-i}[S],\]
Möbius-transform each rank, and take \(h[S]=H_{|S|}[S]\). Terms with overlapping operands cancel under Möbius inversion. Time \(O(n^{2} 2^{n})\) and memory \(O(n2^{n})\).
Use it when the transition partitions a set into two labeled, disjoint parts and \(n\) is around 20. If one side can be enumerated sparsely, \(O(3^{n})\) may be smaller and easier.



On positive integers ordered by divisibility:
\[F[x]=\sum_{d\mid x}f[d],\qquad G[x]=\sum_{x\mid m}f[m].\]
For arrays up to \(N\), the first transform adds from \(i\) to \(ip\) for every prime \(p\). Traverse \(i\) upward in the forward stage and downward in the inverse stage, so chains \(i,ip,ip^2,\ldots\) accumulate and undo correctly. A linear-sieve list of primes makes the structural analogy with subset bits explicit.
These divisor transforms diagonalize LCM convolution: zeta over divisors, multiply, invert. For GCD convolution, use sums over multiples; process \(x\) downward for the forward transform and upward for its inverse. Complexity is \(O(N\log\log N)\) with prime-stage transforms (or \(O(N\log N)\) with direct divisor loops).
Preconditions: indices start at 1; define deliberately whether zero exists. \(\gcd(0,x)\) and \(\operatorname{lcm}(0,x)\) make zero a special element, so most contest implementations handle it separately.




A | B, A & B, and A ^ B require three different transforms; visual similarity is not algebraic equivalence.
Möbius inversion must be performed in the same ring as the sums. Under a modulus, normalize subtraction.
\(O(n^{2} 2^{n})\) subset convolution becomes memory-bound first. Use contiguous rank-major storage.
SOS DP may need only one transformed array, not a convolution. Do not pay for an inverse you do not need.
For counting reachable XORs, a linear basis can beat FWT; FWT is appropriate when multiplicities/distributions matter for every XOR value.

text:

title: 18 — Holonomic (D-Finite and P-Recursive) Methods
text:
The linear recurrences in Chapter 10 have constant coefficients. A sequence is P-recursive when
\[\sum_{j=0}^{r}P_j(n)a_{n-j}=0\]
for fixed polynomials \(P_j\). Over characteristic zero, this is equivalent to its ordinary generating function being D-finite: it obeys a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients. This broader class captures many binomial sums, diagonals, walks, and labelled graph counts. Classical closure theorems are stated in characteristic zero. Computing a derived recurrence modulo a prime is safe only after tracking denominators and separately handling indices where they vanish.


In \(x^{i}F^{(j)}(x)\), coefficient extraction produces falling-factorial polynomials in \(n\). Therefore a differential equation converts mechanically to a P-recurrence, and conversely. Keep enough initial terms and separately handle indices where the leading polynomial vanishes.



D-finite series are closed under addition, multiplication, differentiation, integration, composition with an algebraic series having zero constant term, and diagonal extraction. Every algebraic series is D-finite, but \(\exp(\exp x)\) is a standard warning that arbitrary composition is not closed. Multiple sums of hypergeometric terms are strong candidates for creative telescoping and P-recursiveness.
Useful contest workflow:

derive an OGF/EGF or a fixed-dimensional binomial sum;
prove it lies in a closed D-finite class;
derive the differential equation symbolically, or guess a bounded-order and bounded-degree recurrence from exact terms;
certify the guessed relation algebraically—sample agreement is not proof;
evaluate with the recurrence, treating singular indices explicitly.




For assumed order \(r\) and coefficient degree \(d\), solve a homogeneous linear system for \((r+1)(d+1)\) unknown coefficients using more exact sequence terms than unknowns. Verify on unused terms, then prove from the original expression. This practical route is sometimes called “Min25-BM,” though the recurrence has polynomial rather than constant coefficients.
A fixed-order P-recurrence is a product of companion matrices whose entries are rational functions of \(n\). Direct evaluation is linear in \(N\). Baby-step/ giant-step polynomial matrix products plus fast multipoint shift can obtain a far coefficient in \(\widetilde O(\sqrt N)\) field operations for fixed order/degree, subject to nonvanishing denominators; the hidden logarithmic factors depend on the polynomial-multiplication and shift routines.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
This chapter turns congruences into algorithms. The recurring contest signal is that values are huge but only their residue, multiplicative order, or compatibility across several moduli matters. Work through the sections in order; the final four topics assume factorization from Chapter 02.


Write \(a ≡ b \pmod{m}\) when \(m \mid (a-b)\). Addition and multiplication descend to residue classes, but division is conditional: \(a\) has an inverse modulo \(m\) exactly when \(\gcd(a,m)=1\). Extended Euclid gives integers \(x,y\) with
\[ax+my=\gcd(a,m).\]
Thus, for \(g=\gcd(a,m)\), the linear congruence \(ax ≡ b \pmod{m}\) has no solution if \(g∤b\); otherwise divide by \(g\), invert \(a/g\) modulo \(m/g\), and obtain one residue class modulo \(m/g\) (hence \(g\) solutions modulo \(m\)).
Recognition. A repeated step on a cycle, synchronized clocks, or an equation with a coefficient that may not be invertible is a linear congruence, not “ordinary modular division.”



To merge \(x≡a \pmod{m}\) and \(x≡b \pmod{n}\), substitute \(x=a+mt\). Then
\[mt\equiv b-a\pmod n.\]
It is solvable iff \(\gcd(m,n) \mid b-a\); all solutions form one class modulo \(\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)\). Fold constraints one at a time, normalize each merged residue, and guard the LCM against overflow.
For pairwise coprime prime powers, CRT is a ring isomorphism \(\mathbb Z/(\prod_i p_i^{e_i})\mathbb Z \cong
\prod_i \mathbb Z/(p_i^{e_i})\mathbb Z\). This is why composite-modulus equations should often be solved locally and recombined.



For prime \(p\), every nonzero residue is invertible: \(\mathbb F_p^\times\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\). Consequently:

Fermat: \(a^{p-1}=1\) for \(a≠0\).
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a) \mid p-1\).
A polynomial of degree \(d\) over a field has at most \(d\) roots unless it is zero.
\(x^{k}=a\) can be converted into a linear congruence in exponents after choosing a primitive root.

For composite moduli, nonzero does not imply invertible, polynomial root bounds may fail, and the unit group need not be cyclic. Always identify where primality is used.
The order of \(a\) modulo \(m\), assuming \(\gcd(a,m)=1\), starts at \(\varphi(m)\) (or the Carmichael exponent \(\lambda(m)\)) and removes prime factors \(q\) whenever \(a^{\operatorname{ord}/q}=1\). A primitive root has order \(\varphi(m)\); primitive roots exist exactly for \(m\in\{1,2,4,p^{k},2p^{k}\}\) with odd prime \(p\) and \(k\ge1\).



The \(p\)-adic valuation \(v_p(n)\) is the exponent of \(p\) in \(n\). It linearizes products:
\[v_p(ab)=v_p(a)+v_p(b),\qquad
v_p(n!)=\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor n/p^j\right\rfloor.\]
For sums, \(v_p(a+b)≥\min(v_p(a),v_p(b))\), with equality if the two valuations differ. LTE supplies sharper forms. The most used one is: for odd prime \(p\), \(p|(x-y)\), and \(p∤xy\),
\[v_p(x^{n}-y^{n})=v_p(x-y)+v_p(n).\]
Use valuations when divisibility by a huge power or the number of trailing prime factors is asked. For binomial coefficients,
\[v_p\binom nk=\sum_{j\ge1}\left(\lfloor n/p^{j}\rfloor-\lfloor k/p^{j}\rfloor-\lfloor(n-k)/p^{j}\rfloor\right),\]
equivalently the number of carries when adding \(k\) and \(n-k\) in base \(p\) (Kummer).
Hensel lifting upgrades a root modulo \(p^{k}\) to modulo \(p^{k+1}\). For \(f(r)=0 \bmod p^{k}\), try \(r'=r+t p^{k}\); after linearization solve \(f(r)/p^{k} + t f'(r) ≡ 0 \pmod{p}\). If \(f'(r)≠0 \bmod p\), the lift is unique. If the derivative vanishes, there may be zero or \(p\) lifts—never assume uniqueness.



Given \(a^{x}≡b \pmod{m}\), baby-step giant-step (BSGS) meets in the middle. With \(n=\left\lceil \sqrt{m}\right\rceil\), store baby steps \(a^{q}\), then scan \(b(a^{-n})^{j}\); a collision gives \(x=q+nj\). This field/group version needs \(\gcd(a,m)=1\) and costs \(O(\sqrt{m})\) time and memory.
When \(\gcd(a,m)>1\), extended BSGS repeatedly strips \(g=\gcd(a,m)\). At each stripping step, require \(g|b\), divide \(m,b\) by \(g\), and maintain the accumulated multiplier; check small exponents along the way. This is subtle enough that a known-tested template is preferable in a contest.
Pohlig–Hellman is better when the group order is smooth: solve the logarithm modulo each prime power dividing the order, then CRT the exponent. Its hard part is the largest prime factor, roughly \(O(\sqrt{q})\) group operations.



For odd prime \(p\) and \(a\ne0\), Euler’s criterion gives \(a^{(p-1)/2}\in\{\pm1\}\). Tonelli–Shanks writes \(p-1=q\cdot2^{s}\) with odd \(q\), finds a quadratic non-residue, then cancels the current error inside the \(2\)-power subgroup. Given a non-residue, it runs in \(O(\log p+s^{2})\) modular multiplications; random sampling finds one in expected constant trials.
For general \(x^{k}=a \pmod{p}\), write nonzero values as powers of a primitive root: \(g^{kt}=a\). A discrete logarithm converts this to \(kt≡\log_g(a) \pmod{p-1}\). It has \(\gcd(k,p-1)\) solutions if compatible. Specialized root algorithms avoid a full discrete log; use them when constraints exceed BSGS.



Euler reduction \(a^{e} \bmod m = a^{e \bmod \varphi(m)} \bmod m\) is valid without qualification only when \(\gcd(a,m)=1\). For a tower, recurse through the Carmichael chain \(m, \lambda(m), \lambda(\lambda(m)), \ldots\) and carry an additional boolean saying whether the true exponent has reached the reduction threshold. For a prime power dividing the base, compare the tower with the valuation threshold; for the unit part, reduce by the local Carmichael exponent, then CRT.
For \(x^{k}=a \bmod p\), the discrete-log reduction in Section 6 is conceptual but may be too slow. Fast algorithms split \(p-1\) into its \(\gcd(k,p-1)\) part, invert the coprime exponent part, and extract roots inside the remaining smooth subgroup. Always return and verify all roots or the required canonical root; existence is equivalent to \(a^{(p-1)/g}=1\), where \(g=\gcd(k,p-1)\) for \(a\ne 0\).

Never use Fermat inversion unless the modulus is prime and the denominator nonzero.
Protect multiplication and LCM with __int128; check promised bounds before casting back.
CRT consistency is a divisibility test, not pairwise coprimality.
Distinguish a primitive root of the whole multiplicative group from an \(n\)th root of unity.
In BSGS, clarify whether the smallest solution is required and handle \(x=0\), \(a=0\), and non-coprime cases.
Hensel’s derivative-zero branch and \(p=2\) require separate analysis.

title: 16 — Set Power Series
text:
A set power series is a table \(f[S]\) for every subset of an \(n\)-element universe. Algebraically it is
\[R[x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}]/(x_0^{2},\ldots,x_{n-1}^{2}),\]
so multiplication discards terms that reuse an element. This viewpoint turns partitions into powers and connected-component extraction into logarithms.


\[ (f*g)[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f[T]g[S\setminus T]. \]
Naive evaluation is \(O(3^{n})\). Split coefficients by rank, \(f_k[S]=[|S|=k]f[S]\), apply subset zeta transforms, convolve the rank index at each mask, and Möbius-invert. The result costs \(O(n^{2} 2^{n})\) time and \(O(n2^{n})\) memory. Unlike OR convolution, the two pieces must be disjoint.



When \(g[\varnothing]=0\), \(g^{n+1}=0\). Therefore substituting \(g\) into an exponential generating series \(F(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}F_kz^k/k!\) gives the finite expression
\[F(g)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}F_k\frac{g^{k}}{k!}.\]
Here \(g^{k}/k!\) counts unordered partitions into \(k\) decorated blocks. Thus, when every nonempty object decomposes uniquely into connected components, \(\exp(g)\) builds arbitrary objects from connected ones and the formal logarithm recovers the connected series from the arbitrary-object series. The factorials must be invertible; in small characteristic use a division-free formulation or explicit partition coefficients.
Pointwise Newton/differential recurrences compute polynomial composition, exp, and related operations in \(\Theta(n^{2} 2^{n})\), rather than repeating subset convolution for every power.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
This chapter collects methods that turn an apparently huge integer range into a small algebraic object: a polynomial, a Euclidean recursion, or a continued fraction. They are especially valuable in ICPC because the statement rarely names the method.


A polynomial of degree at most \(d\) is determined by \(d+1\) distinct values. Lagrange interpolation gives
\[P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{d} y_i\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{x-x_j}{x_i-x_j}.\]
At arbitrary points this costs \(O(d^{2})\) for one query. When \(x_i=i\), prefix/suffix products and factorials reduce one query to \(O(d)\) after \(O(d)\) preprocessing:
\[\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{x-j}{i-j}

title: 15 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
This chapter treats \(\mathbb F_p[x]\) the way Chapters 01–02 treat integers. Division, gcd, irreducibility, and factorization work because coefficients form a field.


Normalize every nonzero gcd to monic. Extended Euclid returns \(aA+bB=\gcd(A,B)\) and gives inverses in \(\mathbb F_p[x]/(M)\) exactly when the gcd is one. Modular polynomial exponentiation reduces after each multiplication; with fast multiplication and remainder it is the basic engine below.
For nonconstant \(f\), the quotient \(\mathbb F_p[x]/(f)\) is a field iff \(f\) is irreducible. When \(\deg f=d\), every residue class \(\alpha\) in that field satisfies \(\alpha^{p^d}=\alpha\). This Frobenius structure replaces trial division over all possible polynomial factors.



For \(f' \ne  0\), \(\gcd(f,f')\) contains repeated factors. Separate the square-free parts before randomized splitting. In characteristic \(p\), \(f'=0\) means every nonzero exponent is divisible by \(p\); take the formal p-th root and recurse. Missing this branch is the classic finite-field factorization bug.



The polynomial \(x^{p^{d}}-x\) is the product of all monic irreducibles whose degree divides \(d\). Repeatedly compute Frobenius powers modulo \(f\) and gcds to perform distinct-degree factorization. A block is then a product of irreducibles of one known degree.
For equal-degree factorization, Cantor–Zassenhaus chooses random \(a(x)\) and, for odd \(p\), splits with
\[\gcd\left(f,a^{(p^{d}-1)/2}-1\right).\]
Restart when the gcd is trivial. Over \(\mathbb F_2\), use a trace-style sum rather than the half-order exponent. Berlekamp instead finds the nullspace of the Frobenius map \(h\mapsto h^{p}-h\); for square-free \(f\), its kernel dimension is the number of irreducible factors.



Linear factors are \(\gcd(f,x^{p}-x)\). Factor that square-free component to list roots. Return roots with multiplicities only after square-free decomposition. For every randomized algorithm, the final certificate is deterministic: multiply the monic factors, restore multiplicities, and compare with the monic input.




Coefficients lie in a prime field; composite coefficient moduli invalidate division.
Keep polynomials trimmed and gcds monic.
Polynomial modular exponentiation must reduce degrees after every multiply.
Random splitters need independent retries and a deterministic reconstruction check.
Complexity depends on multiplication \(M(n)\); state whether a routine is naive or NTT-based.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
This chapter is about changing the indexing of a sum: from integers to prime powers, from pairs to their gcd, or from every quotient to the \(O(\sqrt{n})\) distinct values of \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\). Those changes of viewpoint are the core of advanced ICPC number theory.


Trial division is enough only up to roughly \(10^{12}\) for a few inputs. For arbitrary unsigned 64-bit integers, use deterministic Miller–Rabin and Pollard–Rho.


For odd \(n\), write \(n-1=d·2^{s}\), \(d\) odd. If \(n\) is prime, each base \(a\) has \(a^{d}=1\) or reaches \(-1\) while repeatedly squaring. A witness that does neither proves compositeness. Testing bases
\({2, 325, 9375, 28178, 450775, 9780504, 1795265022}\)
is deterministic for all 64-bit inputs. Complexity is \(O(\log n)\) modular multiplications per base.



Iterate a pseudo-random polynomial \(f(x)=x²+c \bmod n\). If two iterates coincide modulo an unknown factor \(p\), then \(\gcd(|x-y|,n)\) reveals a divisor. Floyd/Brent cycle detection and batched gcds make this fast in practice. It is randomized with heuristic expected time about \(O(p^{1/2})\) for a factor \(p\), often described as \(O(n^{1/4})\) for balanced semiprimes.
Pitfalls. Handle \(n<2\); use unsigned 128-bit multiplication; restart Rho when it returns \(n\); recursion receives prime powers as well as semiprimes; randomized runtime has no strict worst-case guarantee.




\(f\) is multiplicative when \(f(1)=1\) and \(f(ab)=f(a)f(b)\) for coprime \(a,b\). It is determined by values on prime powers. Central examples:



\(f(n)\)
prime-power value \(f(p^{e})\)
interpretation




\(\varphi\)
\(p^{e}-p^{e-1}\)
units modulo \(n\)


\(\mu\)
\(-1\) if \(e=1\), else \(0\)
inverse of constant-one function


\(τ\)
\(e+1\)
number of divisors


\(\sigma_k\)
\(1+p^{k}+…+p^{ek}\)
sum of kth powers of divisors



The Euler/linear sieve visits each composite exactly once as \(i·p\), where \(p\) is its least prime factor. It computes primes, \(\mu\), and \(\varphi\) through \(N\) in \(O(N)\) time and memory.



For arithmetic functions,
\[ (f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n} f(d)g(n/d). \]
It is associative and commutative, with identity \(ε(1)=1\), \(ε(n>1)=0\). Convolution preserves multiplicativity. Let \(1(n)=1\); since \(1*\mu=ε\),
\[F(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)F(n/d).\]
This is not a formula to memorize in isolation. Derive it by convolving \(F=f*1\) with \(\mu\). Useful identities follow immediately:
\[1*\varphi=\operatorname{id},\qquad \mu*\operatorname{id}=\varphi,
\qquad 1*1=\tau.\]


If a condition asks for \(\gcd(x,y)=1\), insert
\[[\gcd(x,y)=1]=\sum_{d\mid x,\ d\mid y}\mu(d).\]
The pair sum becomes \(\sum_d \mu(d) A_d B_d\), where \(A_d,B_d\) count multiples of \(d\). More generally, group pairs by their gcd, derive a divisor zeta relation, then invert.




For arrays on \([1,N]\), the divisor zeta transform computes \(F[j]=\sum_{d\mid j}f[d]\). Direct non-in-place divisor loops cost \(N(1+1/2+\cdots+1/N)=O(N\log N)\); inversion follows from the arithmetic Möbius formula. Prime-wise in-place updates compute the transform and its inverse in \(O(N\log\log N)\). For each prime \(p\), the divisor-zeta update \(f[ip]\mathrel{+}=f[i]\) must traverse \(i\) upward so prime powers accumulate; its inverse traverses \(i\) downward while subtracting. The multiple zeta transform \(F[d]=\sum_{d\mid j}f[j]\) reverses the divisibility order. Divisor zeta diagonalizes LCM convolution, while multiple zeta diagonalizes GCD convolution; the more general poset view appears in the transforms chapter.
Recognition. If every operation replaces a set by all divisors, every query involves \(\gcd\), or values are bounded while query count is large, transform the entire frequency vector instead of processing elements individually.



The value \(q=\lfloor n/l\rfloor\) remains constant through
\[r=\left\lfloor n/q\right\rfloor.\]
Thus a loop for (l=1; l<=n; l=r+1) has only \(O(\sqrt{n})\) iterations. The distinct quotients are precisely the small integers up to \(\sqrt{n}\) plus values \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\) for small \(i\).
For two or more floor terms, take the minimum end point: if a summand uses \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\) and \(\lfloor m/i\rfloor\), then \(r=\min(n/(n/l), m/(m/l))\). Pair this with prefix sums of \(\mu\), \(\varphi\), powers, or another arithmetic function.
A standard derivation is
\[\sum_{i=1}^n \left\lfloor\frac ni\right\rfloor
=\sum_{ab\le n}1=\sum_{k\le n}\tau(k),\]
showing how a floor sum and a divisor sum are the same lattice-point count.



If \(f(1)≠0\) in a coefficient field, its Dirichlet inverse exists:
\[g(1)=1/f(1),\qquad
g(n)=-\frac1{f(1)}\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\d>1}}f(d)g(n/d).\]

title: 14 — Modular Combinatorics and q-Analogues
text:
This chapter begins where factorial tables stop working. The two warning signs are \(n \ge  modulus\) and a composite modulus: denominators may vanish, so separate prime valuations from unit parts before dividing.


For prime \(p\), write \(n=\sum n_i p^{i}\) and \(k=\sum k_i p^{i}\). Lucas gives
\[\binom nk\equiv\prod_i\binom{n_i}{k_i}\pmod p.\]
Kummer says \(v_p\binom nk\) is the number of carries in base \(p\) when adding \(k\) and \(n-k\). Lucas is the value theorem; Kummer is the zero/divisibility theorem. A digit with \(k_i>n_i\) is precisely where a carry makes the result zero modulo \(p\).



For \(q=p^{e}\), represent a factorial as \(n! = p^{v} U\), where \(U\) is a unit modulo \(q\). Legendre supplies \(v\); compute the product of integers not divisible by \(p\) in complete blocks, recurse on \(n/p\), and retain the unit modulo \(q\). Then
\[\binom nk=p^{v_p(n!)-v_p(k!)-v_p((n-k)!)}
U(n)U(k)^{-1}U(n-k)^{-1}\pmod {p^e}.\]
If the exponent is at least \(e\), the answer is zero. Otherwise all inverted parts are units. Factor a composite modulus into coprime prime powers, solve locally, and combine with CRT. Never cancel numerator and denominator directly in \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\).



When \(q\) is a prime power, the q-binomial coefficient counts \(r\)-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_q^{n}\):
\[\binom nr_q=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}\frac{q^{n-i}-1}{q^{r-i}-1}.\]
It is also the inversion generating polynomial for binary strings with \(r\) ones, and the area generating polynomial for partitions inside an \(r\times(n-r)\) rectangle. The recurrence
\[\binom nr_q=\binom{n-1}r_q+q^{n-r}\binom{n-1}{r-1}_q\]
remains valid even when the product formula appears to divide by zero. For a fixed numerical \(q\) modulo prime \(P\), precompute q-integers and q-factorials only while their factors are invertible. If some \(q^i-1\) vanishes modulo \(P\), ordinary division is invalid even though the Gaussian binomial itself remains defined. Use the division-free recurrence, a proved q-Lucas theorem when its hypotheses match, or cancel cyclotomic-factor exponents before evaluation.



Factorial-scaled EGF formulas require \(1,\ldots,N\) to be invertible. When \(N\ge p\), use base-\(p\) digit structure, recurrences that avoid division, or algorithms specifically designed for small characteristic. This affects Stirling rows, Bell numbers, FPS integration, and q-factorials—not just \({n\choose k}\).




Prime modulus and \(n<p\): factorial tables.
Small prime and huge \(n\): Lucas; use Kummer to reason about zeros.
Prime power: valuation plus unit factorial.
General composite modulus: prime powers plus generalized CRT.
q-analogue: identify whether it counts subspaces, inversions, or partitions.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Ordinary sieves compute every value through \(N\); summatory sieves compute only
\[F(N)=\sum_{n\le N}f(n)\]
when \(N\) is too large to visit. The art is choosing the correct structure:

Du Jiao sieve: an easy Dirichlet convolution isolates \(F(N)\).
Min_25 sieve: \(f\) is multiplicative and \(f(p)\) is a low-degree polynomial in \(p\).
Powerful-number sieve: remove an easy function agreeing with \(f\) on primes, leaving support only on numbers whose prime exponents are never one.

Before this chapter, master multiplicative functions, Möbius inversion, and quotient grouping in Chapter 02.


Every recursive call in these methods should normally be one of the distinct values \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\). There are fewer than \(2\sqrt{N}\) such values. Two common indexing schemes are:

store large values in a hash map and precompute all values up to a cutoff;
map \(v\) to \(v\) itself if \(v≤\sqrt{N}\), otherwise to \(N/v\) in a second array.

Never accidentally memoize arbitrary arguments: that can turn an intended \(O(\sqrt{N})\) state set into linear space.



Suppose \(h=f*g\) and prefix sums of \(h\) and \(g\) are cheap. Summing the convolution and swapping variables gives
\[H(N)=\sum_{d\le N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If \(g(1)=1\), isolate \(d=1\):
\[F(N)=H(N)-\sum_{d=2}^{N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
Commutativity lets you swap the names of \(f,g\) if the other factor has easier prefix sums. Group equal quotients so that each coefficient sum over a block can be obtained from \(G\).


Let \(M(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\mu(n)\). From \(\mu*1=\varepsilon\), for \(N\ge1\),
\[
M(N)=1-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)M(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
\qquad r_N(l)=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{\lfloor N/l\rfloor}\right\rfloor.
\]
Here \(\mathcal B_N\) is the set of quotient-block starts: begin with \(l=2\) and repeatedly replace \(l\) by \(r_N(l)+1\). It is not the set of every integer from \(2\) through \(N\).
Let \(\Phi(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\varphi(n)\). From \(\varphi*1=\operatorname{id}\), with \(T(N)=N(N+1)/2\),
\[
\Phi(N)=T(N)-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)\Phi(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
\]
with the same definitions of \(\mathcal B_N\) and \(r_N(l)\).
Precompute both functions to \(B\) by linear sieve and memoize only larger quotient states. A cutoff around \(N^{2/3}\) gives the classic practical complexity near \(O(N^{2/3})\), though tuning and the query model affect constants.
The quadratic scale of \(\sum\varphi(n)\) requires wide intermediates. Reduce modulo the problem modulus inside every operation if that is what the statement asks.




Name the wanted prefix \(F\).
Find \(g\) so \(h=f*g\) has an elementary prefix.
Sum \(h(n)\) for \(n≤N\), swap \(n=dk\), and isolate \(F(N)\).
Express coefficient sums on \([l,r]\) with prefix formulas.
Confirm every recursive argument is \(\lfloor N/l\rfloor\) and smaller than \(N\).





Let the distinct quotient states be \(w=N/l\). Initialize
\[g_k(w)=\sum_{i=2}^{w}i^{k}.\]
Process primes \(p\) in increasing order. For every state \(w≥p²\), subtract numbers whose smallest prime factor is \(p\):
\[g_k(w)\mathrel{-}=p^{k}\left(g_k(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)-S_k(p-1)\right),\]
where \(S_k(p-1)=\sum_{q<p,q prime}q^{k}\). After processing all \(p≤\sqrt{N}\), \(g_k(w)=\sum_{q≤w,q prime}q^{k}\).
Why \(p²\)? Any composite still being removed has least prime factor \(p\), hence it is \(p·x\) with \(x≥p\). Why subtract \(S_k(p-1)\)? Those smaller-prime cofactors were never eligible in this stage. Updating states in descending order prevents using values already modified by the current prime.
For \(k=0\), this computes \(\pi(w)\). Its practical complexity for one \(N\) is about \(O(N^{3/4}/\log N)\) time and \(O(\sqrt{N})\) memory.



Assume \(f\) is multiplicative, each \(f(p^{e})\) is computable in \(O(1)\), and
\[f(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}c_kp^{k}\]
for small fixed \(K\). Run the prime-sum sieve for each required power \(k\); combine the arrays to obtain
\[G_f(x)=\sum_{p\le x}f(p).\]
Then enumerate integers by their least prime. Index primes from \(p_0=2\) and set \(G_f(p_{-1})=0\). Define \(S(x,y)\) as the sum of \(f(n)\) for \(2\le n\le x\) whose least prime is at least \(p_y\). Its prime-only base contribution is \(G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})\). For every possible least prime \(p_i\), enumerate its exponent:
\[
S(x,y)=G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})+
\sum_{\substack{i\ge y\\p_i^2\le x}}
\sum_{\substack{e\ge1\\p_i^{e+1}\le x}}
\left(f(p_i^e)S(\lfloor x/p_i^e\rfloor,i+1)+f(p_i^{e+1})\right).
\]

Every recursive call in these methods should normally be one of the distinct values \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\). There are fewer than \(2\sqrt{N}\) such values. Two common indexing schemes are:

title: 11 — Probability and Expectation
text:
Competitive-programming probability is usually deterministic algebra wearing a random story. Define the state precisely, write a one-step equation, and solve the resulting DAG, linear system, or generating function.


For an event \(A\), let \(I_A=[A]\) be 1 when it occurs and 0 otherwise. Then \(E[I_A]=P(A)\). If
\[X=\sum_i [A_i],\qquad E[X]=\sum_iP(A_i),\]
whether the events are independent is irrelevant. This is the first tool for expected inversions, occupied boxes, surviving edges, and distinct values.
Worked example. In a uniformly random permutation of \(n\) items, each pair is inverted with probability \(1/2\). Hence the expected inversion count is \(\binom n2/2\), without describing any transition process.
For products, independence does matter: \(E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]\) is not generally true. Condition instead when dependence is awkward.



Partition outcomes by the next random choice:
\[E[X]=\sum_y P(Y=y)E[X\mid Y=y].\]
The common self-loop pattern is
\[E=s+pE+\sum_iq_iE_i
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
E=\frac{s+\sum_iq_iE_i}{1-p}.\]
Never implement an iterative self-reference before algebraically removing it. If \(p=1\), the target is unreachable and expectation is infinite.
Conditioning can also reduce state: reveal the first special object, the maximum sampled index, or the number of successful trials—whatever makes the remaining process symmetric.



Two equivalent state choices are common:

p[state]: probability of reaching the state; push mass forward and sum terminal rewards.
E[state]: expected remaining cost; pull from successor expectations.

Use probability mass for acyclic processes and distributions; use expectation states when only one moment is needed. State aggregation is the hard part. Exchangeable objects should be represented by counts, not identities: e.g. \((c1,c2,c3)\) plates containing 1, 2, or 3 sushi.
If transitions strictly increase/decrease a measure, topologically order states. Otherwise you have cycles and need equations.



Partition a finite Markov chain into transient states and absorbing states:
\[P=\begin{pmatrix}Q&R\\0&I\end{pmatrix}.\]
Expected hitting times satisfy
\[t=\mathbf1+Qt,\qquad (I-Q)t=\mathbf1.\]
Absorption probabilities satisfy the same left-hand matrix with a different right-hand side. The fundamental matrix \(N=(I-Q)^{-1}\) has N[i][j] equal to the expected number of visits to transient state \(j\) starting at \(i\).
You do not normally invert a matrix explicitly: solve linear systems. Dense cost is \(O(S^3)\). Exploit banded, tridiagonal, monotone, or graph structure. A finite chain has finite hitting expectation precisely when absorption occurs with probability one from the start state.



For an integer-valued random variable \(X\), the probability generating function is
\[G_X(z)=E[z^{X}]=\sum_kP(X=k)z^{k}.\]
Independent sums multiply PGFs. Moreover \(G'_X(1)=E[X]\) and \(G''_X(1)=E[X(X-1)]\), so variance follows from factorial moments. This turns repeated independent dice/steps into polynomial multiplication.
First-step recurrences translate into rational GFs. For a renewal process with step PGF \(A(z)\), geometric repetition often produces \(1/(1-A(z))\). This connects probability DP to formal power series and linear recurrences.




“Uniformly select an available action” changes probabilities as the state changes.
Expected ratio is not ratio of expectations.
Modulo probabilities require all denominators invertible; this models exact rational arithmetic in a field, not floating-point probability.
For double, use pivoting in cyclic systems and avoid subtracting nearly equal probabilities.
An unreachable absorbing state means infinite expectation, not a large finite DP value.
Memoized recursion on a cyclic state graph never resolves the cycle.

title: 08 — Generating Functions and Coefficient Extraction
text:
A generating function (GF) is a modelling language; an FPS is the algebra used to compute it. The critical skill is translating combinatorial construction into an equation before choosing an algorithm.


An ordinary generating function (OGF) stores \(A(x)=\sum a_nx^{n}\). Its product splits an integer size: \([x^{n}]AB=\sum_ia_i b_{n-i}\). Use it for sequences, weights, paths and otherwise unlabelled atoms.
An exponential generating function (EGF) stores \(\widehat A(x)=\sum a_nx^{n}/n!\). Its product distributes a set of labels:
\[
n![x^n]\widehat A\widehat B=\sum_i{n\choose i}a_i b_{n-i}.
\]
Use it when labels are partitioned among components. A useful labelled-class dictionary is:



construction
EGF

\(\log(1/(1-A))\)



The last three require \(A(0)=0\). Examples: permutations are sets of cycles, so their EGF is \(\exp(\log(1/(1-x)))=1/(1-x)\). Set partitions are sets of nonempty sets: \(\exp(e^{x}-1)\).



If \(a_n=\sum_{i=1}^{d} c_i a_{n-i}\), multiply by \(x^{n}\) and sum:
\[
A(x)=\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)},\qquad Q(x)=1-\sum_{i=1}^dc_ix^i,
\]
where P = (initial-prefix * Q) mod x^d. Conversely, a rational OGF gives a constant-coefficient linear recurrence. This equivalence lets you choose among:

DP: \(O(nd)\), good for small \(n\);
polynomial inverse: first \(n\) terms in \(O(M(n))\);
Kitamasa: one huge term in \(O(d^{2}\log n)\);
Bostan–Mori: one huge term in \(O(M(d)\log n)\).




To find \([x^{k}]P(x)/Q(x)\), multiply top and bottom by \(Q(-x)\). The denominator \(Q(x)Q(-x)\) contains only even powers. Keep the numerator powers matching the parity of \(k\), discard the other parity, replace \(x^{2}\) by \(x\), and halve \(k\).
Require \(Q[0]\) to be a unit, reduce \(P \bmod Q\) initially if necessary, and trim degrees after multiplications. Complexity is \(O(M(d)\log k)\).



Recursive objects often give implicit equations. For plane rooted trees whose root has an ordered sequence of subtrees, \(T=x(1+T+T^{2}+\cdots)=x/(1-T)\). Binary trees with allowed node-weight inventory \(W(x)\) give \(F=1+WF^{2}\). Solve algebraically only after specifying the empty object and whether children are ordered.
Some equations can be evaluated with FPS inv/sqrt/exp; others are better used directly for coefficient extraction by Lagrange inversion.



For \(\Phi\in R[[t]]\), the equation \(T(x)=x\Phi(T(x))\) recursively determines a unique \(T\in xR[[x]]\). For \(n>0\) and integer \(k>0\), Lagrange inversion gives
\[
[x^n]T(x)^k=\frac{k}{n}[t^{n-k}]\Phi(t)^n,
\]
and more generally
\[
[x^n]H(T(x))=\frac1n[t^{n-1}]H'(t)\Phi(t)^n.
\]
These divided forms assume that \(n\) is invertible in the coefficient ring. Over characteristic \(p\le n\), the corresponding identity after multiplying through by \(n\) remains valid but may no longer determine the wanted coefficient. Use a small-characteristic method; division by \(n\) is not justified.


Coefficient extraction is a formal residue: \([x^{n}]H(T)=\operatorname{res}_x H(T)x^{-n-1}\). Substitute \(x=t/\Phi(t)\); the formal change-of-variables rule supplies \(dx=(\Phi-t \Phi')/\Phi^{2} dt\). Expanding and integrating the formal derivative term by parts leaves \(\frac1n[t^{n-1}]H'(t)\Phi(t)^{n}\). No analytic convergence is involved.
Worked example. Labelled rooted trees satisfy \(T=x \exp(T)\). Then \([x^{n}]T=\frac1n[t^{n-1}]e^{nt}=n^{n-1}/n!\); multiplying by \(n!\) gives Cayley’s \(n^{n-1}\) rooted labelled trees.
Recognition signal: the unknown appears recursively on both sides, but can be rearranged to \(T=x \Phi(T)\). If the target is one coefficient, do not compute the whole compositional inverse.






Constraints such as \(i=j\) can be enforced by an auxiliary variable: \(\sum_i a_{i,i}x^{i}=\operatorname{CT}_z A(x/z,z)\). Roots-of-unity filters select indices modulo \(m\): over a field in which \(m\) is invertible and which contains a primitive \(m\)th root \(w\),
\[
\sum_{n\equiv r\pmod m}a_nx^n=
\frac1m\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}w^{-rj}A(w^jx).
\]



Products over many factor types become sums: \((\log F)'=F'/F\). For \(F=\prod_k(1-x^{k})^{-c_k}\), \[
[x^{n-1}]F'/F=\sum_{d\mid n} d c_d.
\] Recover \(F\) with FPS exponential or a coefficient recurrence. This is central to partition and multiset enumeration.



An algebraic or exponential GF often satisfies \(A'(x)=B(x)A(x)\) or another coefficient-friendly differential equation. With sparse \(B\), the induced recurrence can beat a general FPS routine.





EGF coefficients contain inverse factorials: usually require \(n < MOD\).
Formal division requires an invertible constant denominator.
\(T=x\Phi(T)\) always determines its zero-constant-term solution recursively. The stronger condition that \(\Phi(0)\) is a unit is needed when treating \(T\) as the compositional inverse of \(t/\Phi(t)\).
Ordered sequence, unordered set and cycle constructions are different.
A closed algebraic expression may introduce a branch; select the constant term dictated by the combinatorial class.
A huge requested index plus small rational denominator signals Bostan–Mori, not expansion through that index.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
text:
Symmetry problems are not “divide by the number of symmetries” problems: some objects have stabilizers. This chapter supplies the correct averaging machinery.


A finite group \(G\) acts on a set \(X\) if \(e\cdot x=x\) and \((gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)\). The orbit \(Gx\) is one equivalence class; the stabilizer \(G_x=\{g:g\cdot x=x\}\). Orbit–stabilizer says \(|Gx||G_x|=|G|\), explaining why naive division fails when stabilizer sizes differ.
Recognition. Build \(G\) explicitly:

necklaces: cyclic group \(C_n\);
bracelets: dihedral group \(D_n\) (rotations and reflections);
grids under rotation: a small geometric permutation group;
colors themselves interchangeable: a second action, often handled by cycle types or another Burnside layer.




Let \(\operatorname{Fix}(g)=\{x:g\cdot x=x\}\). Then
\[
  |X/G|=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{Fix}(g)|.
\]
Proof. Count pairs \((g,x)\) with \(gx=x\). Summing by \(g\) gives the numerator. Summing by each orbit gives \(\sum_{x\in O}|G_x|=|O|\,|G|/|O|=|G|\). Thus every orbit contributes \(|G|\).
For unrestricted \(c\)-colorings of positions, if permutation \(g\) has \(z(g)\) cycles, a fixed coloring is constant on each cycle and contributes \(c^{z(g)}\).


Rotation by \(r\) has \(\gcd(n,r)\) position cycles. Therefore
\[
N(n,c)=\frac1n\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}c^{\gcd(n,r)}
=\frac1n\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(n/d)c^d.
\]
Group rotations by their gcd instead of iterating to \(n\); this is often the difference between \(O(n)\) and \(O(\sqrt n)\) after factoring \(n\).
For bracelets, add reflections. If \(n\) is odd, each reflection has one fixed position and \((n-1)/2\) pairs. If \(n\) is even, half have two fixed positions and half have none. Re-derive these cycles rather than memorising the final formula.




Burnside counts unrestricted colors. To track how many times each color occurs, define
\[
Z_G(s_1,s_2,\ldots)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}
\prod_{j\ge1}s_j^{c_j(g)},
\]
where \(c_j(g)\) is the number of length-\(j\) cycles. Substitute \(s_j\leftarrow y_1^{j}+\cdots+y_c^{j}\). The coefficient of \(y_1^{a_1}\cdots y_c^{a_c}\) counts orbits with exact color multiplicities.
Weighted inventory. If a color/object of weight \(w\) has inventory \(A(x)=\sum_w a_wx^{w}\), substitute \(s_j=A(x^{j})\). Truncate every polynomial to the requested total. This is the operational form most useful in ICPC.



Burnside is only the outer loop. For each group element:

Compute its cycles on atomic positions.
Contract every cycle: all its positions must receive the same state.
Count valid assignments to weighted contracted nodes using DP/GF.
Sum and divide by \(|G|\).

If adjacency constraints are present, contraction may create self-loops or multi-edges. A self-loop can make a proper coloring impossible. For grid states, sometimes it is cheaper to apply the symmetry to transfer-matrix states rather than individual cells.



Fixed counts are constant on conjugacy classes. A permutation of cycle type \(1^{m_1}2^{m_2}\cdots\) has class size
\[
\frac{n!}{\prod_i i^{m_i}m_i!}.
\]
Thus Burnside over \(S_n\) can be a sum over integer partitions of \(n\), not \(n!\) permutations. Generate partitions as multiplicities, compute cycle-induced constraints, and weight by the class size.




Division by \(|G|\) modulo prime \(p\) requires \(p\nmid|G|\). If not, compute the numerator exactly, or modulo a proved multiple of \(p|G|\) that permits the exact integer division, before reducing modulo \(p\); problem-specific cancellation may offer a cheaper route.
The action must preserve validity; otherwise its orbits are irrelevant.
Reflection cycle structures differ by parity.
If colors are indistinguishable, ordinary position Burnside alone still treats color names as distinct.
Exact multiplicities mean coefficient extraction, not simply \(\mathrm{colors}^{\mathrm{cycles}}\).

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
text:
Polynomial multiplication is the engine behind the next two chapters. This chapter explains the contracts behind NTT, arbitrary-mod strategies, division, product trees, evaluation, interpolation and Taylor shift.


For \(C(x)=A(x)B(x)\), \(c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j\). Evaluating at sufficiently many points turns multiplication into pointwise products; interpolation returns the coefficients. FFT uses complex roots of unity, NTT roots in a finite field.
For transform length \(L=2^{s}\), a prime modulus \(p\) must satisfy \(L\mid p-1\) and a primitive \(L\)th root must exist. With \(998244353 = 119*2^{23}+1\), primitive root \(3\), lengths through \(2^{23}\) are available.


Complex FFT needs coefficient splitting and careful rounding. When the target modulus is arbitrary, use enough NTT-friendly primes to reconstruct each integer coefficient by CRT, then reduce modulo the target. The coefficient bound, not the target modulus, determines how many primes are enough; three primes are only a common choice when their product exceeds the proved bound. If only the result modulo \(m\) matters, Garner reconstruction can avoid a huge integer. AtCoder Library’s convolution_ll is a reliable reference for its stated signed-64-bit coefficient range.
Complexity is \(O(n\log n)\) time and \(O(n)\) memory.




If \(\deg A<\deg B\), return \(Q=0\) and \(R=A\). Otherwise, let \(\operatorname{rev}_k(F)\) mean: reverse the full coefficient array of \(F\), then truncate or pad the result to length \(k\). For \(A=BQ+R\), \(\deg R<\deg B\), set \(k=\deg(A)-\deg(B)+1\). Reversal gives
\[
\operatorname{rev}_k(Q) \equiv
\operatorname{rev}_k(A)\,\operatorname{rev}_k(B)^{-1}\pmod{x^k}.
\]
Compute the FPS inverse (chapter 07), reverse back, and set \(R=A-BQ\). This costs \(O(M(n))\). Preconditions: field coefficients and nonzero leading coefficient.



For points \(x_i\), build a balanced tree \(P_v(x)=\prod_{i\in v}(x-x_i)\). At the root compute f mod P_root; descend with remainder mod P_child. At leaf \(i\), the constant remainder is \(f(x_i)\). Fast division at every level yields \(O(M(n)\log n)\).
Naive Horner is better when the degree or number of points is small; fast algorithms have large constants.



For distinct \(x_i\), let \(P(x)=\prod_i(x-x_i)\). Lagrange basis gives
\[
f(x)=\sum_i y_i\frac{P(x)}{(x-x_i)P'(x_i)}.
\]
Evaluate \(P'\) at all points with the product tree. Put \(w_i=y_i/P'(x_i)\) at leaves and merge
\[
F_v=F_LP_R+F_RP_L.
\]
The root is \(f\), in \(O(M(n)\log n)\). Duplicated points make \(P'(x_i)=0\); either reject inconsistent input or use Hermite interpolation.
For a polynomial of degree at most \(n\) known at the consecutive points \(0,\ldots,n\), evaluation at arbitrary \(t\) can be done in \(O(n)\) using prefix/suffix products and \[
f(t)=\sum_i y_i\frac{\prod_{j\ne i}(t-j)}{i!(-1)^{n-i}(n-i)!}.
\]



Find coefficients of \(f(x+c)\). Since
\[
[x^k]f(x+c)=\sum_{i\ge k}a_i{i\choose k}c^{i-k},
\]
multiply by \(k!\) and rewrite as a convolution of reversed \(A_i=a_i i!\) with \(B_j=c^{j}/j!\), then divide the result by \(k!\). This is \(O(M(n))\), assuming factorials are invertible.



Use a priority queue or divide-and-conquer product tree, multiplying similar degrees first. For total output degree \(N\), balanced multiplication is typically \(O(M(N)\log k)\). Always truncate to the maximum requested degree; for knapsack factors this can save orders of magnitude.




Transform length must divide MOD-1; it must also cover a.size+b.size-1.
Normalize negative residues before NTT.
CRT primes must support the same transform length.
Polynomial inverse requires nonzero constant coefficient; division instead relies on the divisor’s leading coefficient.
Multipoint interpolation requires distinct points.

title: 07 — Formal Power Series
text:
An FPS \(A(x)=\sum_{i\ge0}a_ix^{i}\) is algebra in \(R[[x]]\), not an analytic function. We never substitute a real \(x\); we work modulo \(x^{n}\). This viewpoint makes every operation finite and makes Newton iteration natural.
Let \(M(n)\) be polynomial multiplication time, \(O(n\log n)\) with NTT. All operations below truncate immediately to the requested precision.


\[
A'=\sum_{i\ge1}ia_ix^{i-1},\qquad
\int A=\sum_{i\ge0}\frac{a_i}{i+1}x^{i+1}.
\]
Over a prime field, integration through degree \(n\) needs \(n < MOD\).

Suppose \(AB\equiv1\pmod{x^{m}}\). Set \[
B_{new}=B(2-AB)\pmod{x^{2m}}.
\] If \(E=1-AB\) is divisible by \(x^{m}\), then \(1-AB_{new}=E^{2}\), divisible by \(x^{2m}\). Precision doubles; total cost is \(O(M(n))\).
Precision doubling should operate on a truncated copy so that a caller’s longer series is not accidentally destroyed.



The logarithm is immediate:
\[
\log A=\int A'A^{-1}\,dx,
\]
in \(O(M(n))\). Its chosen constant is zero, hence the clean contract \(A[0]=1\).
For exponential, maintain \(B\equiv e^{A}\pmod{x^{m}}\) and correct by \[
B_{new}=B(1+A-\log B)\pmod{x^{2m}}.
\]
The bracket is \(1 \bmod x^{m}\), so known coefficients remain unchanged. Standard implementations are \(O(M(n))\), though careless repeated inversions may add a constant or logarithmic factor.



For \(A(0)=1\), \(A^{k}=\exp(k\log A)\). In general find the first nonzero term \(a_tx^{t}\):
\[
A^k=x^{tk}a_t^k\left(A/(a_tx^t)\right)^k.
\]
If \(tk \ge  n\), the truncated answer is zero. This handles huge nonnegative \(k\) without reducing \(k\) when computing the shift; only exponent arithmetic in the field is reduced.
For square root with invertible \(2B\), Newton gives \[
B_{new}=\frac12(B+A/B).
\] Start with a modular square root of the leading coefficient (Tonelli–Shanks for an odd prime). Strip an even valuation first. A unit series over an odd prime field has exactly two roots, differing by sign. For a positive even valuation, shifting either unit root gives the two canonical roots, but coefficients too high to affect the square modulo \(x^n\) are unconstrained unless the output contract fixes them (normally to zero). Problems must specify a canonical root or accept any valid one.



Naive composition computes powers \(1,B,B^{2},\ldots\) in \(O(nM(n))\). Brent–Kung baby-step/giant-step chooses \(k\approx\sqrt n\):
\[
A(B)=\sum_q B^{qk}\left(\sum_{r<k}a_{qk+r}B^r\right).
\]
Precompute baby powers \(B^{r}\), form each block polynomial, then combine by Horner in \(B^{k}\). A straightforward realization costs roughly \(O(M(n)\sqrt n)\) time and \(O(n\sqrt n)\) memory. Faster algorithms exist, but this decomposition contains the main conceptual step.
The condition \(B[0]=0\) ensures output coefficients below \(n\) depend only on input coefficients below \(n\). With nonzero constant term, a finite FPS prefix does not generally determine the composition.



For \(A(0)=0,A'(0)\ne0\), Newton solve \(A(B)-x=0\):
\[
B_{new}=B-\frac{A(B)-x}{A'(B)}\pmod{x^{2m}}.
\]
This needs composition plus multiplicative inversion. With Brent–Kung it is about \(O(M(n)\sqrt n)\). If only one or a structured set of coefficients is needed, Lagrange inversion (chapter 08) is usually better:
For integers \(1\le k\le n\),
\[
[x^n]B(x)^k=\frac{k}{n}[t^{n-k}]\left(\frac{t}{A(t)}\right)^n.
\]
This divided form requires \(n\) to be invertible in the coefficient field; in small characteristic, use a division-free identity or a method designed for that characteristic.

\[
nb_n=\sum_{i=1}^n i a_i b_{n-i}.
\]
Similarly \(B=A^{-1}\) uses \(b_n=-a_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_{n-i}\). Choose sparse versus dense by estimated work, not merely by degree.



Let \(A=1-x\). Then \(\operatorname{inv}(A) = 1+x+x^{2}+...\), \(\log(A)=-x-x^{2}/2-x^{3}/3-...\), and \(\operatorname{pow}(A,k)\) reproduces \(\sum_i(-1)^{i}{k\choose i}x^{i}\). This tiny example checks signs, integration inverses and truncation.

\(A*\operatorname{inv}(A) = 1 \bmod x^{n}\);

\(\exp(\log(A)) = A\) when \(A[0]=1\);
\(\sqrt{A}^{2} = A\);
\(\operatorname{compose}(A,\operatorname{revert}(A)) = x\).

title: Notation and algebra contracts
text:
The same symbol can denote very different operations in contest editorials. These notes use the following conventions unless a chapter overrides them.



\([x^{n}]F(x)\) is the coefficient of \(x^{n}\).
\(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\) is the ring of residues modulo \(m\).
\(\mathbb F_p\) is a field only when \(p\) is prime.
mint denotes a modular-integer type whose modulus is stated nearby.
Division by \(a\) means multiplication by \(a^{-1}\) and therefore requires that \(a\) be a unit. In \(\mathbb F_p\) this is equivalent to \(a\ne0\); modulo a composite \(m\) it is equivalent to \(\gcd(a,m)=1\).
For nonzero \(n\), \(v_p(n)\) is the exponent of prime \(p\) in \(n\); when needed, \(v_p(0)=+\infty\).





\(\mathbf 1(n)=1\), \(\varepsilon(1)=1\) and \(\varepsilon(n)=0\) for \(n>1\).
\(\mu\), \(\varphi\), and \(\tau\) are the Möbius, Euler-totient, and divisor-count functions.
Dirichlet convolution is \((f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)g(n/d)\); its identity is \(\varepsilon\).
A function is multiplicative when \(f(1)=1\) and \(f(ab)=f(a)f(b)\) for \(\gcd(a,b)=1\); “completely multiplicative” drops the coprimality requirement.





Polynomials and formal power series are coefficient arrays in increasing degree order.
\(F\bmod x^{n}\) means retain degrees \(0,\ldots,n-1\).
Multiplicative inverse \(F^{-1}\) requires \(F(0)\) to be a unit.
Formal \(\log F\) is normalized to constant term zero and normally requires \(F(0)=1\); formal \(\exp F\) normally requires \(F(0)=0\).
Formal composition \(F(G(x))\) is automatically well-defined for arbitrary infinite FPS only when \(G(0)=0\). Truncated or polynomial cases may allow more.
Compositional inverse/reversion requires \(F(0)=0\) and \(F'(0)\) a unit.
NTT length and root-of-unity conditions are part of an algorithm’s contract, not implementation trivia.
\(\binom nr_q\) is a Gaussian/q-binomial coefficient; the subscript is a numerical field size or formal variable, not the arithmetic modulus.
A set power series has coefficients \(F[S]\) and multiplication \((FG)[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}F[T]G[S\setminus T]\).
\(F^{(j)}\) denotes the \(j\)th formal derivative; in a set-series chapter a partial derivative with respect to an element variable is named explicitly.





\(\operatorname{Pf}(A)\) is the Pfaffian of an even skew-symmetric matrix; over characteristic other than two, \(\operatorname{Pf}(A)^{2}=\det A\).
\(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) is the adjugate and satisfies \(A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)I\) even when \(A\) is singular.
A P-recursive sequence satisfies a fixed-order recurrence with polynomial coefficients in the index. A D-finite series satisfies a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients.
Classical D-finite closure statements are characteristic-zero results. Modular computation requires checking every denominator and singular index.





Subsets are bitmasks when the ground set is \([0,n)\).
The subset zeta transform sends \(f(S)\) to \(\sum_{T\subseteq S}f(T)\).
XOR/AND/OR convolution names refer to the operation combining indices, not the pointwise operation after transformation.
“Möbius inversion” may mean inversion on subsets, the divisor poset, or a general locally finite poset. The chapter always names the order relation.





\(M(n)\) denotes the cost of multiplying degree-below-\(n\) polynomials; with a suitable NTT, \(M(n)=O(n\log n)\).
A bound such as \(O(M(n))\) can conceal a large constant and strict modulus requirements. Use the actual maximum degree and transform count when judging feasibility.
Randomized algorithms state whether their guarantee is Las Vegas (always correct, random time) or Monte Carlo (small error probability).





Signed overflow is never intentional. Products near the 64-bit boundary use __int128 or an explicitly justified unsigned technique.
Routine algorithms are assumed to come from the reader’s tested library; the notes state the contracts and arithmetic assumptions needed to select them.
